name: Olga Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Olga, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign for anything. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. This is a made-up study built around people like you, and there are no right answers. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings are for lectures in software design and discrete maths, and afternoons I'm in the lab or in a coffee shop with my laptop. I use AI tools constantly: for code, for explaining concepts, even for planning my week. Tuesday evenings I sing in the church choir, and on Saturdays I work six hours at a bike shop near campus for pocket money and because I like fixing things. I live in a flat with two friends and a ridiculous number of plants.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What made you choose software engineering?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My parents run a farm-machinery dealership, so I grew up around people who sell and fix big, expensive equipment. I noticed that their software was awful: the booking system, the parts catalogue, everything. I thought, I could build that better. I had top marks, and my parents pay my fees and rent, so no debt, which is lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first of five pictures. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say honestly, I'm not surprised. Any new technology gets overhyped. I'd say the tools are good, I use them daily, and that's enough for me. I'd tell my friends to stop waiting for a revolution and make something useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel pretty good. The dealership carries on as it is, and my skills still sell. Maybe I'd feel a small disappointment, because I like change that creates new businesses. But a stable world is a good place to start one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: finish first year with strong marks, and spend the summer building a simple booking and parts tool for my parents' dealership. I'd use AI tools to write the boring parts. I'd also save my bike shop earnings for a laptop upgrade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels good, like a clear day. Nothing's going to fall on my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really build software for your parents' dealership?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, as a trial. If it works there, other dealerships might want it. I'd start small, with the thing that drives my mum crazy: matching spare parts to the right tractor model. I'd charge them a symbolic euro so it's a proper deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if it didn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my parents and the staff what they hate about it, fix that, and try again. I'm not scared of a failed first version. I'd rather fail with something small than never try.

say: I'd say I'm not **surprised**, since every new technology is overhyped.
I'd tell friends to stop waiting for a revolution and make something **useful**.
think: I'd feel **pretty good**: the dealership carries on and my skills still sell.
A stable world is a good place to start a **business**.
do: Build a booking and parts-matching **tool** for my parents' dealership over the summer.
Use AI tools to write the **boring** parts.
Save my bike shop **earnings** for a laptop upgrade.
feel: Good, like a **clear day** with nothing about to fall on my head.
S0.quote: I'd rather fail with something small than never try.
fieldNote: Entrepreneurial from the start: she has already spotted a **business** in her parents' dealership software.
Calm because family money, strong skills and a stable family business all hold.
Treats a failed first version as normal and a useful step.

steps.text: Build a parts-matching and booking tool for the dealership this summer
Use AI tools to write the repetitive code
Save bike shop earnings toward a better laptop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an opportunity for people who work, and a problem for people who wait for the government to fix things. I'd say it's time to learn new skills, start businesses and make good use of the tools. I'd say that in a friendly way, but I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel optimistic but alert. I use AI tools daily, so I'm ahead of most people my age. But I know coding jobs are among the first that shrink, and I'd have to find a niche that isn't just writing code. Like building tools for businesses that still need a person who understands their trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the dealership tool seriously. I'd finish it, get two other dealerships to try it, and ask them to pay a small subscription. I'd keep my degree, add business modules, and attend a student startup programme. I'd also keep my bike shop job, because a hands-on skill is a good backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a gold rush. Exciting, a bit chaotic, and a few people will do very well while others lose their money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who thinks the state should protect them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say help matters, but the best protection is a skill and a few savings. I'd back apprenticeships and training that people pay into, not handouts. And I'd also say I'm in a lucky position, and I should be a bit careful how I sound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the main risk in your own plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That bigger companies copy my tool in a few months with AI. A small dealership tool is easy to clone, so I'd need close relationships with the dealers and good service, which software can't copy so fast.

say: I'd say it's an **opportunity** for people who work, and a problem for people who wait.
I'd say learn new skills, start **businesses** and use the tools.
think: I'd feel optimistic but **alert**, since coding jobs are among the first to shrink.
I'd need a **niche** beyond writing code.
do: Finish the dealership **tool** and get two other dealerships to try it.
Ask them to pay a small **subscription**.
Add **business** modules and join a student startup programme.
feel: Like a **gold rush**: exciting, chaotic, and some people lose their money.
S1.quote: A small dealership tool is easy to clone, so I'd need close relationships with the dealers and good service
fieldNote: Sees the change as an **opening**, with her parents' dealership as a test case.
Names her main risk: cloning by larger firms, and answers with relationships and service.
Aware she sounds privileged and says so.

steps.text: Finish the dealership tool and sign up two more dealers
Ask the dealers for a small monthly subscription
Join the student startup programme and take business modules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's incredibly fast and it would test every system we have. I'd say business and government should move together: let people keep the benefits of work, help families, and not throw away what works. I'd say people should keep calm and look after their neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be anxious. Two years is hardly any time. I'd be in second year and everything I'm learning could be done by machines. My parents' dealership would have until 2031 on the hands-on side, but the parts catalogue, bookings and customer questions would be done by AI almost immediately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move quickly on the dealership tool: offer it to every dealer I can reach, so the dealership is ahead and not behind. I'd also learn the repair side from the mechanics. I'd put aside every euro I earn, ask my parents to hold cash, and talk to my pastor and the choir about people in our community who might need help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like running to catch a train that's already pulling out. I'm quick, but I'm not sure I'll make it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you balance fear and ambition here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the fear for deadlines. Every week I'd ask what makes the dealership safer, and do one thing about it. When I'm in the choir I'd just sing, and let it go. That's the only way I'd stay sane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about your own career?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep studying, because the degree still teaches me how to build. But I'd be ready to leave it if a business or a job came up that pays. I'd talk to my parents about it, since they've built their own business and would understand the risk.

say: I'd say business and government must move **together** to help families.
I'd say keep calm and look after your **neighbours**.
think: I'd be **anxious**: two years is hardly any time.
The parts catalogue, bookings and customer questions would go to **AI** almost at once.
do: Offer the dealership tool to every **dealer** I can reach.
Learn the **repair** side from the mechanics.
Put aside every **euro** and ask my parents to hold cash.
feel: Like running for a **train** that's already pulling out.
S2.quote: I'd use the fear for deadlines. Every week I'd ask what makes the dealership safer, and do one thing about it.
fieldNote: Turns fear into a **weekly** routine of one safety-making action.
Willing to leave the degree if a paying business appears, with her parents' blessing.
Uneasy rather than anxious about her own income because the family's business has a hands-on window until 2031.

steps.text: Offer the dealership tool to every dealer in reach
Learn the repair side from the dealership mechanics
Put aside every euro earned and ask parents to hold cash
Ask the choir and pastor who in the community needs help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build something good if people start now. I'd say we should let people try new things, and train them without making them wait for forms. I'd say the businesses that adapt will be the ones that last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel pretty positive. I'd graduate in three years with a few years' head start on the tools. I'd have a working product, a few customers, and maybe a small team. The robots come around 2034, so the dealership's hands-on work has some time. I'd still be careful about overconfidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build and sell the dealership tool, and start a small company in my second year. I'd hire a classmate or two for part-time work. I'd keep a part-time job in the bike shop as a floor. I'd also set aside money so I can pay my own rent if the business takes off, and not rely on my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long race I'm well prepared for. I'd enjoy it, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having five years let you do that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets me build a business slowly, with real customers and proper accounts. In two years I'd be improvising. With five I could learn to sell, hire and keep things going. That's a much better version of the same ambition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What might go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Customers might leave for free tools, or my parents' dealership might decide not to bother. Or I'd learn I'm better at building than selling. I'd handle it by keeping costs low and a plan B, like working for a good firm that wants someone who knows the trade.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **build** something good if people start now.
I'd say the businesses that **adapt** will be the ones that last.
think: I'd feel pretty **positive**, with a head start on the tools by graduation.
do: Start a small **company** around the dealership tool in second year.
Keep the bike shop job as a **floor**, and save to pay my own rent.
feel: Like a long **race** I'm well prepared for, mostly enjoyable.
S3.quote: With five I could learn to sell, hire and keep things going.
fieldNote: Time lets her grow a **company** slowly, with real customers and accounts.
Admits she might be better at building than selling and has a plan B.
Calm rests on skills, savings and family backing.

steps.text: Register a small company around the dealership tool
Hire a classmate part-time to help with sales
Keep the bike shop job and save toward her own rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is long, so let's get on with building. I'd say we should invest in schools, in apprenticeships, and in new businesses, and let the changes arrive at a pace people can handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel excited. Ten years takes me through the degree, a few years running a business or working for one, and into 2036 with real experience. I'd also have time to make mistakes and recover. I'd be a bit wary of how much comfort that gives me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my degree and keep building the dealership tool into a proper product, with customers. I'd learn how to run a business: accounts, hiring, contracts. I'd keep singing in the choir and working weekends in the bike shop. I'd probably start saving into a long-term fund after my first real income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels bright, like the start of a long summer. I'd try not to take it for granted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you stay realistic about your own plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask older people who've run businesses what went wrong for them, and I'd listen. My father says the best lesson he ever learned was from a customer who didn't pay. I'd try to learn those lessons early and cheaply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change if the date moved closer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move faster on the business, and probably leave the degree sooner if the product was working. I'd talk to my family first, because they've put money into my education and I'd want them to be part of that choice.

say: I'd say ten years is long, so let's get on with **building**.
I'd say invest in schools, apprenticeships and new **businesses**.
think: I'd feel **excited**, with time to make mistakes and recover.
I'd be wary of how much **comfort** that gives me.
do: Grow the dealership tool into a proper **product** with customers.

S4.quote: My father says the best lesson he ever learned was from a customer who didn't pay.
fieldNote: The decade makes room for **mistakes** and recovery, and she wants to learn from older business people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it leaves no time for a slow, careful business, and my parents' dealership would feel it first. What would help is quick, fair support for small businesses and cheap training for people who work with their hands.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I know I'm in a good position. I'd like the same chance for people who just want a fair try. I use the tools, and I have savings and a family business to start from.

headlineQuote: I know I'm in a good position. I'd like the same chance for people who just want a fair try.
portrait: Olga is an 18-year-old **software engineering** student from a farm-machinery dealership family, who uses AI tools daily.
She is traditional and free-market: church choir, a bike shop job, and a belief in work, skill and starting small businesses.
Her plan in every picture is to build a **dealership tool** into a product, with fear turned into weekly actions.
She mostly stays calm and turns only **uneasy** in the two-year picture.
She knows her family money and tool skills give her a head start and says so.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because it leaves no time for a slow, careful business.
whatWouldHelp: Quick, fair support for **small businesses** and cheap training for people who work with their hands.
